title: GPU-Accelerated Computational Infrastructure for Biomedically-Driven Applications
text:
The requested GPU server will significantly enhance public health research by enabling faster, more accurate
analysis of large biomedical datasets, including medical images and sensor data. It will support innovative
projects in wearable health technologies, disease detection, and health informatics, empowering students and
researchers to develop cutting-edge solutions that improve healthcare outcomes and train the next generation
of health tech professionals. This infrastructure will have a direct impact on both biomedical research and
education at UNT, advancing healthcare innovations and preparing students for careers in digital medicine.

title: Synergistic Effects of Dietary Interventions and Probiotics on Gut-Lung Immune Modulation: Exploring Combined Fiber-Rich Diet, Intermittent Fasting, and Probiotic Strategies to Alleviate Lung Inflamma
text:
Each year, 35 million Americans suffer from chronic lung disease, and an additional 200,000
suffer from acute lung injury, which carries a mortality rate of up to 40%. A growing body of
evidence suggests that the gut microbiome significantly influences immune function and
inflammation. By investigating whether a fiber-rich diet and intermittent fasting can
synergistically enhance beneficial metabolite production and reduce lung injury and by
identifying optimal probiotics that further modulate gut-lung interactions, this research may
provide novel non-pharmacological strategies to mitigate inflammatory lung diseases.
Importantly, the findings have the potential to improve respiratory health outcomes, reduce
healthcare burden, and guide future clinical trials for lung disease management.

title: Transposable Elements as Mechano-Response Enhancer Elements Regulating hESC Fate
text:
Transposable elements (TEs), which make up over half of the human genome, are essential gene regulatory
sequences influencing human mRNA expression in health and disease. This project introduces a novel concept:
TEs function as Mechano-Response Enhancer Elements (MREEs) to regulate human gene expression and cell
fate, shedding light on genome-environment interactions and mechanobiology. The discovery of MREEs will
establish a new class of mechano-sensors and effectors in addition to protein coding genes, with far-reaching
implications for both fundamental research and translational applications in TE regulation and mechanobiology
in health and disease.

title: Core C - Renewal  Molecular Informatics Core - Vision Research
text: IV. Molecular Informatics Core Project Summary The Molecular Informatics Module will provide assistance with access to instrumentation necessary for RNA, Protein and Cell Biology studies. In addition it will serve as a service for proteomic and metabolomic/isotopomic research strategies and technologies to the investigators involved in this P30 Cole Eye Vision Research Core. The time required to develop expertise in proteomic and metabolomic technologies often generates research roadblocks to capable investigators with other specialized skills. Specifically, the module will provide 1) access and technical assistance with instrumentation necessary for cell and molecular assays; 2) experimental design consultation, technical support, and data analysis for global and targeted protein quantitation in normal and diseased ocular tissues and cell systems, including proteomic bioinformatics; 3) a centralized resource for proteomic research strategy and technical support for vision science studies involving protein identification, protein-protein interactions and posttranslational modifications; 4) experimental design consultation and technical support for metabolomic profiling in normal and diseased ocular tissues and cell systems; and 5) a centralized resource for metabolomic research strategy and technical support for vision science studies, including metabolomic bioinformatics. This core module will support NEI R01-funded investigators, help newly recruited investigators obtain data for NEI R01 grant submissions, foster collaborative interactions between RO1-funded investigators and newly recruited investigators, attract investigators from other departments to research on the visual system and be a valuable departmental resource in attracting additional vision scientists to our program as we expand our research faculty.

title: Speeding Immune Reconstitution after Thymus Transplantation
text:
In this proposal, we will assess effects of manipulating two of the pathways that regulate the initial robust
growth of the thymus in the perinatal period on thymus growth and the speed and quality of immune
reconstitution post-cultured thymus tissue implantation. Our approaches are translatable and, if successful,
may also speed T cell reconstitution after cancer treatment, advance progress toward generating donor-
specific tolerance to transplanted organs, improve treatment of autoimmunity, and ameliorate age-related
declines in immunity.

title: Tri-I Training Program in Metabolomics
text: This R25 proposal seeks to further develop and expand an established structured didactic and laboratory training program in metabolomics. In doing so, this proposal aims to enhance training of NIAID-funded trainees in this emerging omics-level science.

title: Characterization of uniquely-positioned IL-33-responsive mucosal cells in colitis-associated cancer.
text:
Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) have an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC),
a leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, and the gut mucosal cells and cytokines that mediate the
transition from inflammation to cancer are poorly understood. We found a uniquely-positioned cell population
expressing the IL-33 receptor, ST2, which are phenotypically heterogeneous and located in the subepithelial
space, overlying polyps of mouse models of CAC. The goal of this study is to identify and functionally characterize
these cells, which may serve as potential markers of CAC and can potentially be used as diagnostic and/or
therapeutic tools to prevent and/or manage tumorigenesis in UC patients.

title: Mechanistic underpinnings of PRPS deficiency disorders
text:
Missense mutations in the gene encoding phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase 1 (PRPS1) are the cause
of several inborn errors of metabolism that can have overlapping as well as distinct pathophysiological
manifestations. Here, we will determine the effects of disease-causing variants of PRPS1 on structure and
biochemistry of the PRPS enzyme complex, define the metabolic deregulations that underlie disease
phenotypes, and develop a new therapeutic strategy to overcome PRPS deficiency.

title: CHARACTERIZING THE ROLE OF CENTRAL NUCLEUS OF THE AMYGDALA AND THE HYPOTHALAMIC PARAVENTRICULAR NUCLEUS IN STRESS-AUGMENTEDCARDIOGENIC SYMPATHETIC AFFERENT REFLEX IN THE RAT
text:
The brain’s response to stress, particularly chronic stress, can worsen outcomes related
to the sympathetic nervous system. We will investigate how specific brain regions,
activated by stress, increase nerve activity that affects heart function, potentially making
heart attacks more severe. By identifying these brain areas and the activated pathways,
this research aims to uncover new ways to prevent or reduce the harmful effects of stress
on heart health.

title: Integrated spatial omics to elucidate conserved inflammatory mechanisms of vesicant-induced skin injury
text:
Despite significant research and investment, no FDA approved broad spectrum countermeasures are available
to rapidly mitigate vesicant-induced injury following intentional or accidental chemical exposure. A major
limiting factor in the development of therapies is the lack of a comprehensive understanding of the
inflammatory damage that occurs following cutaneous vesicant exposure. The goal of this proposal is to
implement and establish a state-of-the-art spatial multi-omics platform to investigate conserved mechanisms of
inflammatory damage induced by dermal exposure to sulfur mustard and lewisite vesicant classes in a
clinically relevant porcine skin model.

title: Gabriella Miller Kids First Pediatric Data Resource Center: Advancing Collaborative Platform-Enabled Data-Driven Discovery at the Intersection of Childhood Development and Cancer
text:
The Gabriella Miller Kids First Data Resource Center (Kids First DRC) manages the largest genomic data
resource focused on identifying the causes of pediatric cancer and congenital anomalies. In this phase, the Kids
First DRC will continue their operations with expanded releases, new data ingest infrastructure and an
exploration of AI-readiness, while promoting our data resource to the research community, clinicians, patients,
and their advocates. Through this work, we will continue to maximize the potential for novel discovery and better
understanding across a multitude of pediatric diseases and disorders for clinical translation.

title: Molecular mechanisms underlying organ penetration in disseminated pneumococcal infection
text:
We have learned that capsule serotype influences the translocation rate of Streptococcus pneumoniae across
vascular endothelial cells (VEC) and into organs during bacteremia. Herein we will examine how capsule
impacts attachment, receptor mediated endocytosis, resistance to intracellular killing, and S. pneumoniae
trafficking to the basolateral surface of VEC for organ invasion. Our results will directly impact risk assessment
strategies for escape from serotype-based vaccine design.

title: Engineering Immunostimulatory Spherical Nucleic Acids for B cell adoptive therapy
text:
This project seeks to develop a novel approach to treating advanced PCa through ACT using peripheral B-cellSNA
in combination with ICB. The experiments proposed here are expected to lay the groundwork for a new B cell-
activating cancer therapy that could be readily extended to other types of immunotherapy-refractory solid “cold”
tumors beyond advanced PCa.

title: Epigenetic Regulation of Skin Regeneration
text: Defective wound healing accounts for enormous morbidity and fiscal burden worldwide. Chronological aging of skin is at the foundation of defective wound healing, although little is known regarding the underlying cause of this association. However compelling data indicates that skin stem cells that become deficient as we age are the basis for defective wound healing. Moreover, reversible epigenetic regulation plays a critical role in stem cell health and maintenance. We therefore posit that the fundamental underpinnings of regenerative healing of skin reside in the epigenetic regulation of skin stem cells. Here, we propose to study epigenetic changes in skin regeneration in wound healing and aging, and test a newly discovered form of in vivo epigenetic reprogramming that we predict will reverse the age and restore function to aging stem cells. Thus, the primary goal of this project is to elucidate epigenetic mechanisms of skin stem cell regulation with focus on DNA methylation/hydroxymethylation and histone modification, and to develop novel and practical translational approaches to reprogramming age-related stem cell epigenetic aberrances. We have assembled a synergistic interdisciplinary team of investigators with a history of pioneering discovery in the areas of aging biology, epigenetics, epigenetic reprogramming, skin stem cell biology, dermatopathology and biomarker application. We also have developed experimental models that encompass biodegradable wound healing scaffold development, human skin xenotransplantation, three-dimensional bioprinting, and a mouse model of epigenetically inducible premature aging. Thus, we will leverage multiple points of synergy, experience, and collaborative interaction to tackle the complex and clinically important questions of age-related wound healing deficiency. Most importantly, we will define and test the therapeutic effects of epigenetic reprogramming in our novel and complementary pre-clinical model systems. This proposal presents a new approach of epigenetic reprogramming of functionally deficient aging stem cells to enhance skin regeneration in order to heal chronic wounds in the aging populace. If successful, such an approach could transform the way we think about the aging process and treating age-related skin disorders.

title: Chimeric RNA driven neopeptide vaccine for prevention of breast cancer in germline BRCA1/2 carriers
text:
Overall –Narrative
This preclinical study addresses the overarching challenge of primary prevention of germline BRCA 1/2 driven
breast cancer. Developments in sequencing technology, in genomics and in informatics, coupled with
advances immunotherapy and safe mRNA vaccines provide a timely opportunity to integrate these strategies
to create an innovative new framework for preventing breast cancer. These developments have already paved
the way for immune boosting vaccines for the treatment of cancer; in our application we propose to harness
these same approaches to develop an” off the shelf” vaccine for prevention of BRCA 1/2 associated breast
cancer.

title: Development of genomic resources to determine the genetic basis of insecticide resistance in sandfly vectors
text:
Sandflies from the genus Lutzomyia are vectors of Leishmania, a genus of protozoan parasites that cause
leishmaniasis in humans. The World Health Organization reports around 1,500,000 cases, and 26,000 to
65,000 deaths due to leishmaniasis annually. Our proposal will expand genomic resources for Lutzomyia, while
identifying genomic regions under selection, with emphasis on uncovering genetic variation that underlies
variation in vector insecticide resistance.

title: Examination of the longitudinal impact of within- and between-day fluctuations in food parenting practices on child dietary intake
text:
This innovative study seeks to understand how the use of specific food parenting practices varies across time
and context, and how various food parenting approaches impact children’s dietary intake over the long term. A
longitudinal study with 240 parent-child pairs will be conducted with data collection via state-of-the-art
measures, including EMA and interview-led 24-hour diet recalls, every 6 months for two years. The proposed
study represents a significant and necessary next step to inform the development of clinic-based
recommendations and public health interventions that account for- and are responsive to- daily challenges
found to influence parent’s use of specific food parenting practices.

title: Red-shifted voltage indicators for two-photon all-optical physiology and multi-spectral imaging
text:
To understand the brain in health and disease, identifying functional connections between neurons is essential. Optogenetics
(to turn on neurons) and voltage biosensors (to read-out brain activity) are powerful tools for achieving this, but the current
spectral compatibility between blue-absorbing voltage sensors and optogenetic reagents poses a limitation. This project
proposes developing red voltage biosensors that operate on a different part of the spectrum, thereby overcoming this
challenge and allowing experiments that provide new insights into how the brain works.

title: Quantitative background parenchymal enhancement, measured on contrast-enhanced mammogram, as a novel marker of breast cancer risk
text:
Background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) is a promising new marker of breast cancer risk that has been
studied almost exclusively using magnetic resonance imaging, an expensive screening modality that is
indicated primarily for women with high risk of breast cancer. We propose here to measure BPE quantitatively
using contrast-enhanced mammogram (CEM), a rapidly emerging screening modality that is more affordable
and generalizable than MRI and assess the potential of BPE measured on CEM as a marker of breast cancer
risk. Our long-term goal is to use our new, objective measure of BPE on CEM to improve assessment of breast
cancer risk, enabling personalization of breast cancer screening to detect breast cancer earlier and ultimately
reduce breast cancer mortality for women in the United States.

title: Improving anti-tumor immunity in advanced breast cancer by targeting solid stress
text:
Our objective is to determine if angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs) can enhance T cell infiltration into breast
tumors and if this enhancement, when combined with cancer immunotherapy, can effectively reduce breast
cancer progression. To accomplish this, we will measure T cell infiltration and function directly in mouse breast
cancer models and we will also evaluate human breast cancer tissue samples to explore the potential synergy
between ARBs and cancer immunotherapy. This research is of critical importance, considering the alarming
annual toll of over 40,000 American lives claimed by breast cancer.
